pages.text:
*Ama's Stall Ledger, Night 18. Bowls sold: 60. Vegetarian customers turned away: 1. Lin's mood: bad.*

Hui-Ting had been walking with me down the lane for six years. She is tall and quiet, with two long braids and glasses that catch the lantern light. Every Friday, she walks past stall nineteen. Every Friday, she never stops.

On Night 18, the first day of the lunar month, she stopped. She stood in front of our counter, looking at the steam rising from the great pot. Her stomach let out a sound that was very loud and very honest.

I held out a bowl. "You must be hungry. Take this."

Hui-Ting shook her head. She looked at the bowl, then at my face, then back at the bowl. "I can't eat this, Lin."

I frowned. "It is just beef noodles. I made them. They are good."

"They are good," she agreed softly. "But today is the first day. My grandmother says I have to eat *su shi*."

I stared at her. I had known Hui-Ting since we were in first grade. I knew she liked rainy days and always had two spare erasers. I did not know that she had a secret rule about soup.

"I thought vegetarian meant no meat," I said.

Hui-Ting smiled, a small, patient smile. "It is a little more than that."
pages.image: Hui-Ting, a tall girl with two long braids and glasses, stands politely in front of a steaming beef noodle stall counter, shaking her head gently while Lin, a smaller girl in a red-and-white checked apron, looks confused and holds out a bowl.

pages.text:
"You have to understand," Hui-Ting said, leaning on the counter. "My grandmother's family believes in being very calm. She says some foods stir up the senses. They make you too excited, or too angry, or too loud."

I thought of Uncle Feng shouting jokes. I thought of my own heart beating when I burn a scallion.

"Which foods?" I asked.

"Garlic. Onion. Chives. Leeks. And green onions," she listed, tapping her fingers on the steel counter. "Her family calls them the five pungent things. They are strong. They wake you up. But on the first and fifteenth days of the moon, my family wants to be still."

I looked at our stall. The air was thick with the smell of ginger and soy sauce. I remembered the basket of green onions behind the pot. I remembered how Ama chopped them, fast and sharp, into the oil until they sizzled.

I had spent my whole life thinking vegetarian meant "no beef." I had never thought about the onions. I had never thought about the garlic. I looked at the kitchen, and for the first time, it did not look like a kitchen. It looked like a wall.

"So," I said, my voice very small. "You can't eat the soup."
pages.image: Hui-Ting, a tall girl with glasses and braids, leans on a metal counter explaining something with gentle hand gestures, while Lin, a shorter girl with a pencil behind her ear, looks down at a basket of green onions with a shocked expression.

pages.text:
I felt heat climb up my neck and wiped my dry hands on my apron anyway. "I can make you plain rice," I offered quickly. "And pickled vegetables from the pickle stall at the end of the lane. They have good pickles."

Hui-Ting nodded, not looking disappointed but kind, which was somehow worse. I walked to the end of the lane and brought back a small bowl of white rice with a plate of crisp, purple pickled cabbage. I set it in front of her, then returned to my table to pick up my own bowl of beef noodles.

The broth was dark and rich. I lifted my spoon and took a sip, letting the tangerine peel release a sharp, sweet scent that hit the back of my nose. It tasted like pride, like work, and like being the best at what I did.

Across the table, Hui-Ting ate her plain rice and chewed slowly, looking happy. I swallowed, and the soup felt heavy in my mouth. It felt like I was eating the wall all by myself.

pages.text:
I put my spoon down and watched the steam curl out of my bowl, twisting into shapes that looked like questions.

"What if," I said, and the word came out louder than I meant it to, so I clamped my mouth shut immediately.

Hui-Ting turned to look at me, her eyes wide behind her glasses.

"What if there was a broth," I whispered, moving my hands as if I were mixing an invisible pot. "No beef. No onions. No garlic. Just dried shiitake mushrooms, and kelp, and roasted tomatoes, and... the eight-spice pouch from Mr. Tsai."

I looked at her, feeling like I was trying to catch a slippery eel in a net made of smoke.

"It would be clear," I said. "And warm. And it would smell like the market, but not like beef."

Hui-Ting was quiet for a long moment while the noise of the market swelled around us, with Uncle Feng laughing and Auntie Ping pouring tea. Then she leaned forward, her voice soft but very steady.

"I would come every week," she said.
pages.image: Lin, a small girl with bright eyes, leans forward across a table speaking intently to Hui-Ting, a taller girl with glasses, who listens with a calm, attentive expression, while steam rises from bowls in the background. All shop signs, banners and hanging boards are smooth plain solid-color cloth.

pages.text:
I didn't wait for a response. I ran to the back of the stall, where Ama was wiping down the metal shelves with a rag that was almost as gray as the floor. She was humming that old song with no words, the one that sounds like a kettle just before it boils.

"Ama," I said, still catching my breath. "What if we made a vegetarian broth? Just mushrooms and kelp and tomatoes? For Hui-Ting?"

Ama stopped humming. She turned to look at me, her face calm and serious, holding the cloth in both hands.

"Beef noodle soup without beef," she said slowly. "That is a fish without water."

"It is not beef noodle soup," I said, trying to keep my voice even. "It is something new. A new kind of soup."

Ama set the cloth on the shelf. She looked at me, and then she looked at the great pot, which was still bubbling quietly in the dark.

"Something new," she said. "That is how you lose something old."

She turned back to her work and picked up the cloth again. She did not hum. I stood there, holding my apron strings, and I did not hum either. The silence between us felt thick, like day-old rice.
